title: Drama
overview: Is unit mein Greek tragedy se lekar Elizabethan, Restoration, 18th-19th century, modern British, American, Irish, Absurd, Indian English aur world drama tak sab aata hai, saath mein dramatic terms bhi. NET mein zyada sawal author-work matching, chronology, characters, famous quotes aur terms ke coiner par aate hain.

topics.title: Greek Tragedy and Aristotle's Poetics
points: Three great Greek tragedians: Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides (chronological order).
Aeschylus: Oresteia trilogy (458 BC) - Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers, The Eumenides; Prometheus Bound; added the second actor.
Sophocles: Oedipus Rex (c. 429 BC), Antigone (c. 441 BC), Electra, Oedipus at Colonus; added the third actor.
Euripides: Medea (431 BC), Hippolytus, The Trojan Women, The Bacchae (405 BC); famous for frequent use of deus ex machina.
Greek tragedies were staged at the City Dionysia in Athens as tetralogies: three tragedies plus one satyr play.
Aristotle's Poetics (c. 335 BC): tragedy is 'the imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude' producing catharsis through pity and fear.
Six parts of tragedy (Aristotle): plot (mythos), character, thought, diction, song (melos), spectacle (opsis). Plot is 'the soul of tragedy'.
Aristotle insisted only on unity of action; unities of time and place were formulated by Castelvetro (1570) - neo-classical rule of three unities.
Key Aristotelian terms: hamartia, peripeteia, anagnorisis, catharsis, mimesis; Oedipus Rex is his model tragedy.
Nietzsche, The Birth of Tragedy (1872): tragedy born from Apollonian and Dionysian forces (Apollo = form, Dionysus = ecstasy).

topics.title: Greek and Roman Comedy; Seneca
points: Old Comedy: Aristophanes - The Clouds (423 BC, satirises Socrates), The Birds (414 BC), Lysistrata (411 BC), The Frogs (405 BC, contest of Aeschylus and Euripides).
Parabasis: in Old Comedy the chorus directly addresses the audience on the poet's behalf.
New Comedy: Menander (Dyskolos / The Grouch) - domestic plots, stock characters; model for Roman comedy.
Roman comedy: Plautus (Menaechmi - source of Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors; Miles Gloriosus - braggart soldier) and Terence (The Eunuch, The Brothers).
Seneca (c. 4 BC - AD 65): closet tragedies like Thyestes, Medea, Phaedra - five acts, ghosts, revenge, bloodshed, rhetorical speeches.
Senecan tragedy shaped Elizabethan revenge tragedy: Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy, Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus and Hamlet.
Horace, Ars Poetica: drama should have five acts; 'decorum'; violence not to be shown on stage (Medea should not kill her children before the audience).
Stock characters from Roman comedy: miles gloriosus (braggart soldier), parasite, clever slave, senex (old man) [purane fixed type ke kirdar].

topics.title: Medieval English Drama
points: Drama re-emerged from church liturgy: the Easter trope 'Quem Quaeritis' (Whom do you seek?) c. 10th century.
Mystery / Miracle plays: Bible-based cycles staged by trade guilds on pageant wagons at Corpus Christi - York, Chester, Wakefield (Towneley), N-Town cycles.
The Second Shepherds' Play (Wakefield cycle, by the 'Wakefield Master') - Mak the sheep-stealer; mixes farce with the Nativity.
Morality plays: allegorical personified virtues and vices - The Castle of Perseverance (c. 1425), Mankind, Everyman (late 15th c.).
Everyman: summoned by Death; only Good Deeds accompanies him to the grave; Fellowship, Kindred and Goods desert him.
Vice: comic tempter figure of moralities - ancestor of Iago and Richard III.
Interludes: short secular plays - John Heywood's The Four PP; Henry Medwall's Fulgens and Lucrece (c. 1497), the earliest known secular English play.
Ralph Roister Doister (Nicholas Udall, c. 1553): first regular English comedy; Gammer Gurton's Needle: early English comedy (c. 1553-60).
Gorboduc (Thomas Sackville and Thomas Norton, 1561/62): first English tragedy in blank verse, Senecan model, with dumb shows.

topics.title: University Wits, Kyd and Marlowe
points: University Wits: John Lyly, George Peele, Robert Greene, Thomas Lodge, Thomas Nashe, Christopher Marlowe (Thomas Kyd often grouped with them though not a university man).
John Lyly: courtly prose comedies Campaspe, Endimion; euphuism (from his prose romance Euphues, 1578).
George Peele: The Old Wives' Tale, The Arraignment of Paris, David and Bethsabe.
Robert Greene: Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay, James IV; in Greene's Groatsworth of Wit (1592) attacked Shakespeare as an 'upstart crow, beautified with our feathers'.
Thomas Kyd: The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587) - founded English revenge tragedy; Hieronimo, ghost, play-within-play; probable author of a lost Ur-Hamlet.
Marlowe: Tamburlaine the Great (c. 1587), Doctor Faustus (c. 1592), The Jew of Malta (c. 1589, Barabas), Edward II (c. 1592), Dido Queen of Carthage.
Ben Jonson praised 'Marlowe's mighty line' - Marlowe perfected dramatic blank verse.
'Was this the face that launched a thousand ships / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?' - Faustus on Helen of Troy.
'Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it' - Mephistopheles in Doctor Faustus.
Marlowe's heroes are over-reachers (Harry Levin, The Overreacher, 1952) driven by lust for power, knowledge, wealth.

topics.title: Shakespeare
points: First Folio (1623) compiled by John Heminges and Henry Condell: 36 plays in Comedies, Histories, Tragedies; Ben Jonson's tribute 'He was not of an age, but for all time'.
Globe Theatre built 1599 by the Lord Chamberlain's Men (King's Men from 1603).
Major tragedies: Hamlet (c. 1600-01), Othello (c. 1603-04), King Lear (c. 1605-06), Macbeth (c. 1606); also Romeo and Juliet, Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra, Coriolanus.
Problem plays (term by F. S. Boas, 1896): Measure for Measure, All's Well That Ends Well, Troilus and Cressida.
Romances / last plays: Pericles, Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale, The Tempest (c. 1611).
Quotes: 'Frailty, thy name is woman' (Hamlet); 'The quality of mercy is not strained' (Portia, Merchant of Venice); 'All the world's a stage' (Jaques, As You Like It).
Quotes: 'Life's but a walking shadow... a tale told by an idiot' (Macbeth); 'O brave new world' (Miranda, The Tempest); 'Ripeness is all' (Edgar, King Lear).
Coleridge on Iago: 'the motive-hunting of motiveless malignity'; Johnson, Preface to Shakespeare (1765): Shakespeare is 'the poet of nature'.
A. C. Bradley, Shakespearean Tragedy (1904): studies Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth; character-based criticism.
T. S. Eliot, 'Hamlet and His Problems' (1919): called Hamlet 'most certainly an artistic failure'; coined objective correlative.
Jan Kott, Shakespeare Our Contemporary (1964); G. Wilson Knight, The Wheel of Fire (1930).

topics.title: Jacobean and Caroline Drama
points: Ben Jonson: comedy of humours - Every Man in His Humour (1598), Volpone (1606), Epicoene (1609), The Alchemist (1610), Bartholomew Fair (1614); also masques with Inigo Jones.
Volpone characters: Volpone (fox), Mosca (fly), Voltore (vulture), Corbaccio (raven), Corvino (crow) - beast-fable names.
John Webster: The White Devil (1612, Vittoria Corombona, Flamineo) and The Duchess of Malfi (c. 1613-14; Bosola, Ferdinand, the Cardinal).
'Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle: she died young' - Ferdinand; 'I am Duchess of Malfi still' - the Duchess.
T. S. Eliot: 'Webster was much possessed by death / And saw the skull beneath the skin' (Whispers of Immortality).
The Revenger's Tragedy (1606, now attributed to Middleton, earlier to Tourneur) - Vindice.
Middleton and Rowley, The Changeling (1622) - Beatrice-Joanna and De Flores; Middleton, Women Beware Women; A Chaste Maid in Cheapside.
John Ford: 'Tis Pity She's a Whore (pub. 1633) - incest of Giovanni and Annabella; The Broken Heart.
Beaumont and Fletcher: Philaster, The Maid's Tragedy; Beaumont: The Knight of the Burning Pestle (1607) - early metatheatrical parody.
Thomas Dekker: The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599, Simon Eyre); Marston: The Malcontent (1603-04); Massinger: A New Way to Pay Old Debts (Sir Giles Overreach).
Puritans closed the theatres in 1642; they reopened with the Restoration of Charles II in 1660.

topics.title: Restoration Drama (1660-1700)
points: After 1660 two patent companies (Killigrew and Davenant); women actresses appeared on the English stage for the first time.
Comedy of manners: witty, cynical comedies of fashionable London - Etherege, Wycherley, Congreve, Vanbrugh, Farquhar.
George Etherege: The Man of Mode (1676) - Dorimant (rake), Sir Fopling Flutter (fop).
William Wycherley: The Country Wife (1675) - Horner, Margery Pinchwife, 'china scene'; The Plain Dealer (1676).
William Congreve: The Old Bachelor (1693), Love for Love (1695), The Way of the World (1700) - Mirabell, Millamant, Lady Wishfort, the 'proviso scene'.
Vanbrugh: The Relapse (1696), The Provoked Wife (1697); Farquhar: The Recruiting Officer (1706), The Beaux' Stratagem (1707).
Aphra Behn: The Rover (1677) - first English woman to earn a living by writing.
Heroic drama (rhymed couplets, love vs honour): Dryden's The Conquest of Granada (1670-71), Aureng-Zebe (1675); Dryden's All for Love (1677) is in blank verse on Antony and Cleopatra.
The Rehearsal (1671) by the Duke of Buckingham satirised heroic drama through the character Bayes (Dryden).
Thomas Otway: Venice Preserv'd (1682), The Orphan.
Jeremy Collier, A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage (1698) attacked Restoration comedy.

topics.title: Eighteenth-Century Drama
points: Sentimental comedy: Colley Cibber's Love's Last Shift (1696) regarded as the first; Richard Steele's The Conscious Lovers (1722) the classic example.
John Gay: The Beggar's Opera (1728) - first ballad opera; Macheath, Polly Peachum; satire on Walpole; source of Brecht's The Threepenny Opera (1928).
Joseph Addison: Cato (1713), neo-classical tragedy; George Lillo: The London Merchant (1731) - domestic/bourgeois tragedy.
Henry Fielding's political satires (Tom Thumb 1730, The Historical Register) led to Walpole's Licensing Act of 1737 - the Lord Chamberlain's censorship.
Oliver Goldsmith: 'An Essay on the Theatre; or, A Comparison Between Laughing and Sentimental Comedy' (1773) attacked sentimental comedy.
Goldsmith: The Good-Natur'd Man (1768), She Stoops to Conquer (1773) - Marlow, Kate Hardcastle, Tony Lumpkin; subtitle 'The Mistakes of a Night'.
R. B. Sheridan: The Rivals (1775) - Mrs Malaprop (malapropism), Lydia Languish, Captain Absolute, Bob Acres.
Sheridan: The School for Scandal (1777) - Lady Sneerwell, Joseph and Charles Surface, the 'screen scene'; The Critic (1779), a burlesque of theatre.
David Garrick: leading actor-manager of Drury Lane; revived naturalistic Shakespeare acting.

topics.title: Nineteenth-Century Drama: Romantics to Wilde and Shaw
points: Romantic poets wrote closet/poetic drama: Shelley's The Cenci (1819) and Prometheus Unbound (1820, 'lyrical drama'); Byron's Manfred (1817); Coleridge's Remorse; Wordsworth's The Borderers.
Popular stage dominated by melodrama and spectacle; Theatres Act 1843 ended the patent theatres' monopoly.
T. W. Robertson: Caste (1867), Society - realistic 'cup-and-saucer' drama.
Arthur Wing Pinero: The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893); Henry Arthur Jones: Mrs Dane's Defence - English problem plays.
Oscar Wilde: Lady Windermere's Fan (1892), A Woman of No Importance (1893), An Ideal Husband (1895), The Importance of Being Earnest (1895), Salome (written in French).
The Importance of Being Earnest: 'A Trivial Comedy for Serious People'; Jack Worthing, Algernon, Lady Bracknell ('A handbag?'), Gwendolen, Cecily; Bunburying.
G. B. Shaw: The Quintessence of Ibsenism (1891); Widowers' Houses (1892), Mrs Warren's Profession (1893), Arms and the Man (1894), Candida (1894).
Shaw: Man and Superman (1903, Life Force; 'Don Juan in Hell' interlude), Major Barbara (1905), Pygmalion (1913, Henry Higgins, Eliza Doolittle), Heartbreak House (1919), Saint Joan (1923).
Shaw won the Nobel Prize in 1925; mocked the well-made play as 'Sardoodledom'.
Edwardian realism: John Galsworthy - Strife (1909), Justice (1910); Harley Granville-Barker - The Voysey Inheritance; J. M. Barrie - Peter Pan (1904).

topics.title: Modern and Contemporary British Drama
points: Verse drama revival: T. S. Eliot - Murder in the Cathedral (1935, Becket, Four Tempters, Chorus of Women of Canterbury), The Family Reunion (1939), The Cocktail Party (1949); Christopher Fry - The Lady's Not for Burning (1948).
John Osborne, Look Back in Anger (Royal Court, 8 May 1956): Jimmy Porter, Alison, Cliff, Helena - launched the 'Angry Young Men'.
Kitchen-sink drama: Arnold Wesker's trilogy (Chicken Soup with Barley, Roots, I'm Talking About Jerusalem); Shelagh Delaney's A Taste of Honey (1958).
Harold Pinter: The Room (1957), The Birthday Party (1958, Stanley), The Caretaker (1960, Davies), The Homecoming (1965), Betrayal (1978, reverse chronology); Nobel 2005.
Tom Stoppard: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead (1966), Jumpers (1972), Travesties (1974), Arcadia (1993).
John Arden: Serjeant Musgrave's Dance (1959); Edward Bond: Saved (1965, stoning of a baby) and Lear (1971); Robert Bolt: A Man for All Seasons (1960).
Peter Shaffer: Equus (1973), Amadeus (1979); Joe Orton: Entertaining Mr Sloane (1964), Loot (1965); Alan Ayckbourn: The Norman Conquests.
Theatres Act 1968 abolished the Lord Chamberlain's stage censorship.
Caryl Churchill: Cloud Nine (1979), Top Girls (1982, Marlene), Serious Money (1987) - feminist and Brechtian techniques.
1990s 'in-yer-face theatre' (Aleks Sierz): Sarah Kane's Blasted (1995), Mark Ravenhill's Shopping and F***ing (1996).
Other names: David Hare (Plenty), Michael Frayn (Copenhagen, Noises Off), Hanif Kureishi (Borderline).

topics.title: Irish Drama
points: Irish Literary Theatre founded 1899 by W. B. Yeats, Lady Gregory and Edward Martyn; Abbey Theatre, Dublin, opened 1904 (funded by Annie Horniman).
Yeats: Cathleen ni Houlihan (1902, with Lady Gregory), On Baile's Strand (1904), At the Hawk's Well (1916, Noh-influenced), Purgatory (1938).
J. M. Synge: In the Shadow of the Glen (1903), Riders to the Sea (1904, Maurya loses all her sons to the sea), The Playboy of the Western World (1907).
The Playboy of the Western World (Christy Mahon, Pegeen Mike) caused riots at the Abbey in January 1907.
Sean O'Casey's Dublin trilogy: The Shadow of a Gunman (1923), Juno and the Paycock (1924), The Plough and the Stars (1926, also caused riots).
Juno and the Paycock: 'Captain' Jack Boyle and Joxer Daly; 'The whole worl's in a terrible state o' chassis.'
Samuel Beckett (Irish, wrote in French and English): Waiting for Godot (French 1953, English 1955), Endgame (1957), Krapp's Last Tape (1958), Happy Days (1961); Nobel 1969.
Brendan Behan: The Quare Fellow (1954), The Hostage (1958).
Brian Friel: Philadelphia, Here I Come! (1964), Faith Healer (1979), Translations (1980, first Field Day production, Ordnance Survey of Ballybeg), Dancing at Lughnasa (1990).
Later: Tom Murphy, Frank McGuinness (Observe the Sons of Ulster...), Marina Carr, Martin McDonagh (The Beauty Queen of Leenane).

topics.title: American Drama
points: Provincetown Players (1915-16) launched Eugene O'Neill and Susan Glaspell (Trifles, 1916 - feminist one-act).
O'Neill: Beyond the Horizon (1920, Pulitzer), The Emperor Jones (1920), The Hairy Ape (1922, Yank - expressionism), Desire Under the Elms (1924), Strange Interlude (1928).

O'Neill: Mourning Becomes Electra (1931, Oresteia set in post-Civil War New England), The Iceman Cometh (1946, Hickey), Long Day's Journey into Night (written 1941, staged 1956; Tyrone family); Nobel 1936.
Elmer Rice: The Adding Machine (1923, Mr Zero); Clifford Odets: Waiting for Lefty (1935); Thornton Wilder: Our Town (1938, Stage Manager), The Skin of Our Teeth (1942).
Tennessee Williams: The Glass Menagerie (1944, memory play - Tom, Laura, Amanda Wingfield), A Streetcar Named Desire (1947 - Blanche DuBois, Stanley Kowalski, Stella), Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1955).
'I have always depended on the kindness of strangers' - Blanche DuBois.

Arthur Miller: All My Sons (1947), Death of a Salesman (1949 - Willy Loman, Biff, Happy, Linda), The Crucible (1953, Salem witch trials as allegory of McCarthyism; John Proctor), A View from the Bridge (1955).
Miller's essay 'Tragedy and the Common Man' (1949): the common man is as apt a subject for tragedy as kings.
Edward Albee: The Zoo Story (1959), The American Dream (1961), Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1962 - George, Martha, Nick, Honey).

African American drama: Lorraine Hansberry, A Raisin in the Sun (1959, title from Langston Hughes' 'Harlem'); Amiri Baraka, Dutchman (1964); Ntozake Shange, for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf (1976, choreopoem).
August Wilson's Pittsburgh (Century) Cycle of ten plays: Ma Rainey's Black Bottom, Fences (1985, Troy Maxson), The Piano Lesson.
Later: Sam Shepard - Buried Child (1978), True West; David Mamet - Glengarry Glen Ross (1983); Tony Kushner - Angels in America (1991-93).

topics.title: Theatre of the Absurd
points: Term coined by Martin Esslin in The Theatre of the Absurd (1961); philosophical basis in Albert Camus' The Myth of Sisyphus (1942).
Features: no logical plot, circular structure, breakdown of language, meaningless waiting, man's existence without purpose.
Waiting for Godot: Vladimir (Didi), Estragon (Gogo), Pozzo, Lucky, a Boy; subtitle 'a tragicomedy in two acts'; opens with 'Nothing to be done.'
Vivian Mercier: Godot is a play in which 'nothing happens, twice'.
Endgame characters: Hamm, Clov, Nagg and Nell (in dustbins); Krapp's Last Tape: Krapp and his tape recorder; Happy Days: Winnie buried in a mound.
Eugene Ionesco: The Bald Soprano (1950, 'anti-play' - the Smiths and the Martins), The Lesson (1951), The Chairs (1952), Rhinoceros (1959, Berenger).
Jean Genet: The Maids (1947), The Balcony (1956), The Blacks; Arthur Adamov; Fernando Arrabal.
Esslin included Pinter, N. F. Simpson and Edward Albee (The Zoo Story, The American Dream) among absurdists.
Precursors: Alfred Jarry's Ubu Roi (1896), Pirandello, Kafka, Dada and Surrealism.

topics.title: European and World Drama
points: Henrik Ibsen ('father of modern drama'): Peer Gynt (1867), A Doll's House (1879, Nora's door slam), Ghosts (1881), An Enemy of the People (1882), The Wild Duck (1884), Hedda Gabler (1890), The Master Builder (1892).
August Strindberg: The Father (1887), Miss Julie (1888, its Preface is a naturalist manifesto), A Dream Play (1902), The Ghost Sonata (1907) - expressionist.
Anton Chekhov: The Seagull (1896), Uncle Vanya (1899), Three Sisters (1901), The Cherry Orchard (1904, Ranevskaya, Lopakhin); staged by Stanislavski's Moscow Art Theatre (founded 1898).
Luigi Pirandello: Six Characters in Search of an Author (1921), Henry IV (1922) - metatheatre; Nobel 1934.
Bertolt Brecht: The Threepenny Opera (1928), Mother Courage and Her Children (1939, staged 1941), Life of Galileo, The Good Person of Szechwan, The Caucasian Chalk Circle - epic theatre.
Federico Garcia Lorca's rural trilogy: Blood Wedding (1932), Yerma (1934), The House of Bernarda Alba (1936).
Jean-Paul Sartre: No Exit / Huis Clos (1944) - 'Hell is other people'; Friedrich Durrenmatt: The Visit (1956).
Wole Soyinka (Nigeria, Nobel 1986): The Lion and the Jewel (1959), A Dance of the Forests (1960), The Road (1965), Death and the King's Horseman (1975, Elesin, Olunde).
Athol Fugard (South Africa): The Blood Knot, Sizwe Bansi Is Dead (1972), 'Master Harold'... and the Boys (1982).
Derek Walcott (St Lucia, Nobel 1992): Dream on Monkey Mountain (1967), Ti-Jean and His Brothers, Pantomime.
Ngugi wa Thiong'o with Micere Mugo: The Trial of Dedan Kimathi (1976); with Ngugi wa Mirii: I Will Marry When I Want (Ngaahika Ndeenda, 1977); Ama Ata Aidoo: The Dilemma of a Ghost (1965).

topics.title: Indian Drama (Classical and Indian English)
points: Bharata's Natyashastra: earliest Indian treatise on drama; rasa theory (8 rasas; shanta added later as ninth); roles of sutradhara and vidushaka.
Kalidasa: Abhijnanashakuntalam (translated into English by Sir William Jones, 1789), Vikramorvashiyam, Malavikagnimitram; Sudraka: Mricchakatika (The Little Clay Cart); Bhasa: Svapnavasavadatta.
Rabindranath Tagore: Chitra (1913), The Post Office (Dak Ghar; Amal), Red Oleanders (Raktakarabi), Sacrifice, The King of the Dark Chamber.

Early Indian English drama: Krishna Mohan Banerji's The Persecuted (1831) - first Indian English play; Sri Aurobindo: Perseus the Deliverer; Harindranath Chattopadhyaya; Asif Currimbhoy: Inquilab, The Doldrummers.

Girish Karnad: Yayati (1961), Tughlaq (1964), Hayavadana (1971; from Kathasaritsagara via Thomas Mann's The Transposed Heads), Naga-Mandala (1988), Tale-Danda (1990), The Fire and the Rain (Agni Mattu Male); Jnanpith 1998.
Vijay Tendulkar (Marathi): Silence! The Court Is in Session (Shantata! Court Chalu Aahe, 1967; Leela Benare), Ghashiram Kotwal (1972, Nana Phadnavis), Sakharam Binder (1972), Kamala (1981).
Badal Sircar (Bengali): Evam Indrajit (1963), Pagla Ghoda; founder of 'Third Theatre' (anganmanch / street-and-courtyard theatre).
Mohan Rakesh (Hindi): Ashadh Ka Ek Din (1958, on Kalidasa), Adhe Adhure (1969); Habib Tanvir: Charandas Chor (1975); Mahesh Elkunchwar: Wada Chirebandi.
Mahesh Dattani: Dance Like a Man (1989), Tara (1990, conjoined twins), Bravely Fought the Queen (1991), Final Solutions (1993), On a Muggy Night in Mumbai (1998).
Dattani was the first Indian English playwright to win the Sahitya Akademi Award (1998) for Final Solutions and Other Plays.
Manjula Padmanabhan: Harvest (1997, organ trade; Onassis Prize); Gurcharan Das: Larins Sahib; Poile Sengupta: Mangalam; Partap Sharma: A Touch of Brightness.

topics.title: Dramatic Theory and Criticism
points: Philip Sidney, An Apology for Poetry (pub. 1595): defended the unities and mocked 'mongrel tragicomedy'.
John Dryden, An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668): dialogue of Crites (ancients), Eugenius (moderns), Lisideius (French) and Neander (English; Dryden himself).
Samuel Johnson, Preface to Shakespeare (1765): rejected unities of time and place - 'the spectators are always in their senses'; defended mixing of tragedy and comedy.
Hegel: tragedy as collision of two equally justified rights (Antigone vs Creon).
Gustav Freytag, Technique of the Drama (1863): pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, catastrophe/denouement.
Emile Zola, 'Naturalism in the Theatre' (1881); Stanislavski's system (An Actor Prepares) - basis of Method acting.
Antonin Artaud, The Theatre and Its Double (1938): Theatre of Cruelty.
Jerzy Grotowski, Towards a Poor Theatre (1968); Peter Brook, The Empty Space (1968) - deadly, holy, rough and immediate theatre.
Augusto Boal, Theatre of the Oppressed (1974): forum theatre, spect-actor.
George Steiner, The Death of Tragedy (1961); Raymond Williams, Modern Tragedy (1966); Lionel Abel, Metatheatre (1963); Eric Bentley, The Life of the Drama (1964).

terms.hindi: नायक की गलती या भूल जो उसके पतन का कारण बनती है
terms.net: Aristotle's term (Poetics) for the error, mistake or 'missing the mark' in judgement by which a tragic hero falls from prosperity to misery; loosely rendered as 'tragic flaw'.

terms.hindi: घमंड, हद से ज़्यादा अहंकार
terms.net: Excessive pride or self-confidence that leads the protagonist to ignore divine warnings or moral law; in Greek tragedy a common form of hamartia.

terms.hindi: किस्मत का अचानक उलटा पलटना
terms.net: Aristotle's 'reversal of situation': a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, as when the messenger in Oedipus Rex brings news meant to cheer but which ruins him.

terms.hindi: सच की पहचान, आँखें खुलना
terms.net: Aristotle's 'recognition' or discovery: a change from ignorance to knowledge, ideally coinciding with peripeteia, as in Oedipus' recognition of his identity.

terms.hindi: मन का शुद्धिकरण, भावनाओं का बाहर निकलना
terms.net: Aristotle's term for the purgation (or purification/clarification) of pity and fear which tragedy effects in the audience (Poetics, Ch. 6).

terms.hindi: नकल, जीवन का अनुकरण
terms.net: Imitation or representation of reality; Plato condemned art as imitation of an imitation, while Aristotle defined tragedy as mimesis of an action.

terms.hindi: मंच पर समूह जो गाकर घटना पर टिप्पणी करता है
terms.net: In Greek drama a group of performers who sing, dance and comment on the action; reduced in Elizabethan drama to a single prologue-speaker (Henry V) and revived by Eliot in Murder in the Cathedral.

terms.hindi: अंत में अचानक आकर समस्या सुलझाने वाला दैवी हस्तक्षेप
terms.net: 'God from the machine': a god lowered by crane to resolve the plot, frequent in Euripides; any improbable contrivance to resolve a plot. Aristotle criticised it.

terms.hindi: एक-एक पंक्ति में तेज़ नोक-झोंक वाला संवाद
terms.net: Dialogue in alternate single lines, often in argument, used in Greek and Senecan tragedy and imitated by Elizabethans (e.g. Richard III, Hamlet).

terms.hindi: समय, स्थान और कार्य की एकता का नियम
terms.net: Neo-classical rules of action, time (one day) and place (one locale), formulated by Castelvetro (1570) from Aristotle, who prescribed only unity of action; rejected by Johnson in the Preface to Shakespeare (1765).

terms.hindi: नाटक का मुख्य पात्र
terms.net: The chief character of a play (Greek protagonistes, 'first actor'); opposed by the antagonist; the deuteragonist and tritagonist are second and third actors.

terms.hindi: अकेले मंच पर अपने मन की बात ज़ोर से कहना
terms.net: A speech in which a character alone on stage utters thoughts aloud, revealing inner mind to the audience, e.g. Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be'.

terms.hindi: दर्शक सच जानते हैं, पात्र नहीं
terms.net: A situation in which the audience shares knowledge of which a character is ignorant, so that the character's words carry a meaning beyond his understanding; tragic irony when it foreshadows doom (Oedipus Rex).

terms.hindi: गंभीर दृश्य के बीच हँसी का पल
terms.net: A humorous scene or character in a serious play that relieves tension and often heightens tragic effect, e.g. the Porter in Macbeth, the Gravediggers in Hamlet.

terms.hindi: बदले पर आधारित खूनी त्रासदी
terms.net: Elizabethan-Jacobean genre derived from Seneca, established by Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy: ghost, revenge for murder, feigned madness, play-within-play and a bloody catastrophe; e.g. Hamlet, The Revenger's Tragedy.

terms.hindi: चालाक, बेईमान षड्यंत्रकारी खलनायक
terms.net: Stock Elizabethan villain modelled on a popular distortion of Machiavelli's The Prince: a cunning, ruthless schemer, e.g. Barabas (The Jew of Malta, whose prologue Machevil speaks), Iago.

terms.hindi: दुनिया से नाराज़, कड़वा व्यंग्य करने वाला पात्र
terms.net: A cynical, discontented railer of Jacobean drama, named from Marston's The Malcontent (1603-04); e.g. Bosola, Flamineo.

terms.hindi: दुख और सुख मिला हुआ नाटक
terms.net: A play mixing tragic and comic elements, threatening disaster but ending happily; Guarini's theory; Beaumont and Fletcher's Philaster; Sidney called it 'mongrel'; Beckett subtitled Godot 'a tragicomedy'.

terms.hindi: राज दरबार का संगीत-नृत्य वाला भव्य नाटक
terms.net: A courtly entertainment of poetry, music, dance and spectacle with masked performers, perfected by Ben Jonson and designer Inigo Jones; Milton's Comus (1634) is a famous example.

terms.hindi: मास्क से पहले का हास्य या भद्दा दृश्य
terms.net: A grotesque or comic interlude preceding the main masque as a foil, introduced by Ben Jonson (The Masque of Queens, 1609).

terms.hindi: बाइबिल की कहानियों पर आधारित मध्ययुगीन नाटक
terms.net: Medieval vernacular drama dramatising Biblical history from Creation to Doomsday, performed in cycles (York, Chester, Wakefield, N-Town) by trade guilds; distinct from miracle plays on saints' lives.

terms.hindi: गुण-दोष को पात्र बनाकर शिक्षा देने वाला नाटक
terms.net: Allegorical drama of the 15th-16th centuries in which personified virtues and vices contend for the soul of Mankind, e.g. Everyman, The Castle of Perseverance.

terms.hindi: एक खास सनक वाले पात्रों की कॉमेडी
terms.net: Comedy developed by Ben Jonson (Every Man in His Humour, 1598) in which each character is dominated by one ruling passion or eccentricity, based on the medieval physiology of four humours.

terms.hindi: ऊँचे समाज के तौर-तरीकों पर चुटीली कॉमेडी
terms.net: Witty, satirical comedy of the sophisticated upper class, centring on intrigue, sexual wit and repartee; typified by Restoration comedy (Etherege, Wycherley, Congreve) and later Sheridan and Wilde.

terms.hindi: आँसू और नैतिकता वाली भावुक कॉमेडी
terms.net: 18th-century comedy that sought tears rather than laughter, showing virtuous middle-class characters rewarded; Cibber's Love's Last Shift, Steele's The Conscious Lovers; attacked by Goldsmith.

terms.hindi: प्रेम और सम्मान के टकराव वाला भव्य नाटक
terms.net: Restoration tragedy in heroic couplets dealing with conflicts of love and honour amid epic grandeur, e.g. Dryden's The Conquest of Granada; satirised in Buckingham's The Rehearsal (1671).

terms.hindi: लोकगीतों की धुनों वाला व्यंग्य संगीत नाटक
terms.net: A comic play with songs set to popular ballad tunes, originated by John Gay's The Beggar's Opera (1728).

terms.hindi: आम घर-परिवार के लोगों की त्रासदी
terms.net: Tragedy of ordinary middle-class or lower-class people in private life rather than kings, e.g. Arden of Faversham, Lillo's The London Merchant (1731); ancestor of modern realist tragedy.

terms.hindi: पढ़ने के लिए लिखा नाटक, मंच के लिए नहीं
terms.net: A play written to be read rather than performed, e.g. Seneca's tragedies, Milton's Samson Agonistes, Shelley's Prometheus Unbound, Byron's Manfred.

terms.hindi: कसे हुए प्लॉट वाला सूत्रबद्ध नाटक
terms.net: Pièce bien faite: a tightly constructed play with careful exposition, suspense, a scène à faire and logical resolution, perfected by Eugène Scribe and Victorien Sardou; mocked by Shaw as 'Sardoodledom'.

terms.hindi: सामाजिक समस्या या उलझी नैतिकता वाला नाटक
terms.net: (1) Drama treating a social problem for discussion, after Ibsen (Shaw, Galsworthy); (2) F. S. Boas's term (1896) for Shakespeare's Measure for Measure, All's Well and Troilus and Cressida.

terms.hindi: जीवन को बिना सजाए हूबहू दिखाना
terms.net: A movement presenting life as determined by heredity and environment with documentary exactness; Zola, 'Naturalism in the Theatre' (1881); Strindberg's Preface to Miss Julie (1888); Antoine's Théâtre Libre.

terms.hindi: बाहरी सच नहीं, मन के भीतर की भावना दिखाना
terms.net: Early 20th-century anti-realist mode distorting the outer world to project inner states, using types, episodic scenes and stylised dialogue: Strindberg's A Dream Play, Kaiser, O'Neill's The Hairy Ape, Rice's The Adding Machine.

terms.hindi: मंच और दर्शक के बीच की अदृश्य दीवार
terms.net: The imaginary wall of a box-set through which the audience watches the action in realist theatre; 'breaking the fourth wall' means addressing the audience directly.

terms.hindi: दर्शक को सोचने पर मजबूर करने वाला ब्रेख्त का रंगमंच
terms.net: Non-Aristotelian theatre of Erwin Piscator and Bertolt Brecht, using episodic narrative, songs, placards and direct address to make the audience think critically rather than identify emotionally.

terms.hindi: दर्शक को भावनाओं में बहने से रोकना
terms.net: Brecht's Verfremdungseffekt (V-effect): techniques that make the familiar strange so the audience stays critically detached and sees social conditions as changeable.

terms.pron: थि-ए-टर ऑफ़ द ऐब-सर्ड (THEE-uh-ter of thee ab-SURD)
terms.hindi: जीवन की निरर्थकता दिखाने वाला बेतुका नाटक
terms.net: Martin Esslin's term (1961) for post-war drama of Beckett, Ionesco, Genet, Adamov, Pinter and others which presents the human condition as meaningless, abandoning logical plot and language; rooted in Camus' The Myth of Sisyphus.

terms.hindi: हँसी के बीच छिपा डर और ख़तरा
terms.net: Irving Wardle's phrase (1958), adapted from David Campton's subtitle, for plays such as Pinter's The Birthday Party where comic everyday talk is shot through with unexplained threat.

terms.hindi: मज़दूर वर्ग के घरेलू जीवन का यथार्थ नाटक
terms.net: Late-1950s British realist drama of working-class domestic life, e.g. Osborne's Look Back in Anger, Wesker's Roots, Delaney's A Taste of Honey; term borrowed from painting criticism.

terms.hindi: दर्शक को झकझोरने वाला शारीरिक, अनुष्ठानिक रंगमंच
terms.net: Antonin Artaud's concept (The Theatre and Its Double, 1938) of theatre that assaults the senses through sound, light, gesture and ritual rather than text, to shatter the audience's complacency.

terms.hindi: बिना साज-सज्जा, सिर्फ़ अभिनेता पर टिका रंगमंच
terms.net: Jerzy Grotowski's theatre (Towards a Poor Theatre, 1968) stripped of costume, sets and lighting effects, centred on the actor-spectator relationship.

terms.hindi: नाटक के भीतर नाटक, खुद को नाटक मानने वाला
terms.net: Lionel Abel's term (Metatheatre, 1963) for drama aware of its own theatricality, as in the play-within-the-play (The Mousetrap in Hamlet), Pirandello and Stoppard.

terms.hindi: किसी पात्र की यादों के रूप में चलने वाला नाटक
terms.net: Tennessee Williams's term for The Glass Menagerie (1944), in which the action is filtered through the narrator Tom's memory, hence non-realistic and dimly lit.

terms.hindi: कविता, नृत्य और संगीत मिला नाट्य रूप
terms.net: Ntozake Shange's term for her form combining poetry, dance, music and song, as in for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf (1976).

terms.hindi: चौंकाने वाला, हिंसक और खुला नाटक
terms.net: Aleks Sierz's label (In-Yer-Face Theatre, 2001) for 1990s British drama of shock and explicit violence and sex: Sarah Kane, Mark Ravenhill.

terms.hindi: कथानक की पाँच सीढ़ियाँ
terms.net: Gustav Freytag's model (Technique of the Drama, 1863) of dramatic structure: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe (denouement).

terms.hindi: कहानी की गुत्थी का अंत में सुलझना
terms.net: 'Unknotting': the final unravelling of the plot after the climax, when complications are resolved; called catastrophe in tragedy.

terms.hindi: नाटक से मिलने वाला भाव-आनंद
terms.net: Bharata's Natyashastra concept of the aesthetic emotion relished by the spectator, arising from vibhava, anubhava and vyabhichari bhava; eight rasas, with shanta added later (Abhinavagupta).

terms.hindi: नाटक का सूत्रधार, कथा जोड़ने वाला
terms.net: 'Holder of the strings': the stage-manager-narrator of Sanskrit drama who opens the play, revived by modern Indian playwrights such as Karnad (the Bhagavata in Hayavadana) and Tendulkar (Ghashiram Kotwal).

terms.hindi: गली-आँगन का मुफ़्त, साधारण रंगमंच
terms.net: Badal Sircar's alternative theatre combining folk and Western forms, performed free in open spaces (anganmanch) without proscenium or elaborate sets.

mcqs.q: Arrange in chronological order: (a) Look Back in Anger (b) A Doll's House (c) Murder in the Cathedral (d) Waiting for Godot (English)
Who among the following was NOT one of the University Wits?
mcqs.exp: Jonson was not a University Wit; Greene, Peele, Nashe, Lyly, Lodge and Marlowe were.

mcqs.q: The phrase 'comedy of menace' is most closely associated with the early plays of:
mcqs.exp: Irving Wardle applied it to Pinter's The Birthday Party (1958).

mcqs.q: Match List I with List II: (a) Volpone (b) The Changeling (c) The Duchess of Malfi (d) 'Tis Pity She's a Whore -- (i) John Webster (ii) John Ford (iii) Ben Jonson (iv) Middleton and Rowley
mcqs.exp: Volpone-Jonson, Changeling-Middleton and Rowley, Malfi-Webster, 'Tis Pity-Ford.

mcqs.q: Mrs Malaprop, whose verbal blunders gave English the word 'malapropism', is a character in:
mcqs.exp: Sheridan's The Rivals (1775).

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): Goldsmith opposed the vogue of sentimental comedy. Reason (R): In 'An Essay on the Theatre' he compared laughing and sentimental comedy and favoured the former.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.exp: The 1773 essay is Goldsmith's direct argument against sentimental comedy.

mcqs.q: The famous 'proviso scene' between Mirabell and Millamant occurs in:
mcqs.exp: Congreve's The Way of the World (1700), Act IV.

mcqs.q: In Dryden's An Essay of Dramatic Poesy, which speaker represents Dryden's own views?
mcqs.exp: Neander defends English drama and is Dryden's spokesman.

mcqs.q: A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage (1698) was written by:
mcqs.exp: Jeremy Collier attacked Restoration comedy in 1698.

mcqs.q: Girish Karnad's Hayavadana draws on Kathasaritsagara and on which work?
mcqs.exp: Karnad acknowledged Mann's The Transposed Heads, itself from the Vetala tale.

mcqs.q: Mahesh Dattani became the first Indian English playwright to win the Sahitya Akademi Award (1998) for:
mcqs.exp: The award was for Final Solutions and Other Plays.

mcqs.q: Which play provoked riots at the Abbey Theatre, Dublin, in 1907?
options: The Playboy of the Western World
mcqs.exp: Synge's Playboy offended nationalists in January 1907.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT part of Sean O'Casey's Dublin trilogy?
mcqs.exp: Red Roses for Me (1942) is a later play.

mcqs.q: Arthur Miller defended the tragic stature of characters like Willy Loman in the essay:
mcqs.exp: Miller's 1949 New York Times essay.

mcqs.q: 'I have always depended on the kindness of strangers' is spoken by:
mcqs.exp: Blanche's last line in A Streetcar Named Desire (1947).

mcqs.q: The term 'Theatre of the Absurd' was coined by:
mcqs.exp: Esslin's book The Theatre of the Absurd (1961).

mcqs.q: Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect) is a key concept of:
mcqs.exp: Brecht's epic theatre aims at critical detachment.

mcqs.q: Which play did Ionesco subtitle an 'anti-play'?
mcqs.exp: La Cantatrice chauve (1950) is called an anti-pièce.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Aristotle's six constituent parts of tragedy?
mcqs.exp: The six are plot, character, thought, diction, song, spectacle; catharsis is the effect.

mcqs.q: The first English tragedy written in blank verse is:
mcqs.exp: Gorboduc (1561) by Sackville and Norton.

mcqs.q: Who referred to Shakespeare as an 'upstart crow, beautified with our feathers'?
mcqs.exp: Greene's Groatsworth of Wit (1592).

mcqs.q: Match the playwright with the play: (a) Vijay Tendulkar (b) Badal Sircar (c) Mohan Rakesh (d) Habib Tanvir -- (i) Evam Indrajit (ii) Charandas Chor (iii) Ghashiram Kotwal (iv) Ashadh Ka Ek Din
mcqs.exp: Tendulkar-Ghashiram Kotwal, Sircar-Evam Indrajit, Rakesh-Ashadh Ka Ek Din, Tanvir-Charandas Chor.

mcqs.q: Match Nobel laureate dramatists with the year of award: (a) G. B. Shaw (b) Eugene O'Neill (c) Samuel Beckett (d) Wole Soyinka -- (i) 1969 (ii) 1986 (iii) 1925 (iv) 1936
mcqs.exp: Shaw 1925, O'Neill 1936, Beckett 1969, Soyinka 1986.

mcqs.q: 'Hell is other people' is a line from:
mcqs.exp: Garcin's line in Sartre's Huis Clos (1944).

mcqs.q: Arrange Shaw's plays chronologically: (a) Pygmalion (b) Saint Joan (c) Arms and the Man (d) Man and Superman
The family at the centre of O'Neill's Long Day's Journey into Night is:
mcqs.exp: James, Mary, Jamie and Edmund Tyrone.

mcqs.q: Brecht's The Threepenny Opera (1928) is an adaptation of:
mcqs.exp: Based on John Gay's ballad opera (1728).

mcqs.q: Walpole's Licensing Act of 1737 was provoked largely by the political satires of:
mcqs.exp: Fielding's satires such as The Historical Register led to the Act.

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): Dr Johnson defended Shakespeare's neglect of the unities of time and place. Reason (R): Johnson held that spectators are always in their senses and know that the stage is only a stage.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.exp: Preface to Shakespeare (1765) argues exactly this.

mcqs.q: Match the critical term with its coiner: (a) Objective correlative (b) Problem play (for Shakespeare) (c) In-yer-face theatre (d) Metatheatre -- (i) Lionel Abel (ii) Aleks Sierz (iii) F. S. Boas (iv) T. S. Eliot
mcqs.exp: Eliot 1919, Boas 1896, Sierz 2001, Abel 1963.
